en: Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa. He who is the lord of all aesthetic delights, the exhalation of the auspicious ones, the refuge of all sages, and the weapon against the darkness of the fickle-minded;
May the seven-horsed Sun be served—he who fulfills all the rites of people through sacrifice and charity, and who illumines the entire world. 1.
Having bowed to his guru, Vaidyanātha, renowned as Pāyaguṇḍe,
explains the *Śrīsūryaśataka* composed by Mayūra for the pacification of diseases.

In this regard, the essence of the aesthetic delight arising from the context of the *Śrīraviśataka* (The Hundred Verses on the Glorious Sun), which was respectfully imbibed from the lotus-like mouths of ancient people, is now being expressed.
[It concerns] the sovereign of the Mālava country, whose capital was Avantikā, and who adorned the assemblies of poets.

The two ancient poets from the East, Bāṇa and Mayūra— jewels upon the crowns of poets and esteemed members of the court of the illustrious Mahārāja Śrī Harṣavardhana, who was renowned for his refined taste as a crest-jewel among poets, a wish-fulfilling tree for supplicants, and a patron of the poet Dhāvaka— existed at that time.

For instance, Mayūrabhaṭṭa was his father-in-law, and Bāṇabhaṭṭa, the author of the *Kādambarī*, was his son-in-law. Between the two of them, there was an intense mutual rivalry regarding their poetic compositions.

Having already learned of this situation, the world-renowned [Bāṇa], having been repeatedly summoned with great respect by the King, once arrived at that capital city and approached the presence of the King. Thereupon, with great honor and extreme courtesy, he was invited by the King along with his retinue to reside in his own palace.
He was established by him in his own temple,

and having stayed there, he spent several days. Then, while engaged in the composition of poetry, the king, having respectfully drunk in the verses of Mayūra, summoned with great longing that same renowned,
virtuous, and long-standing poet who had mastered all that is to be known— Mayūrabhaṭṭa— as he had been before.

Adorned by a circle of disciples and accompanied by a retinue of horses, chariots, camels, palanquins, and other attendants, he arrived at Avantikā. Upon hearing of his arrival, the king— preceded by the visit of his ministers' sons, the family priest, and others— welcomed him with great honor and affection into the most beautiful upper chamber of Bāṇabhaṭṭa’s palace.

He was quickly gratified by the provision of well-perfumed food, clothing, and other necessities. Then Mayūrabhaṭṭa, having performed his daily duties there at the proper time—such as bathing, the twilight prayers, and the worship of the gods—sat upon a comfortable seat surrounded by his disciples. Having eaten according to his desire, he remained for some time in great contentment, recounting stories related to ancient kings. Then [he beheld] that which clung to the crown of the peak of the Western Mountain...

Having observed the orb of the sun and performed the final rites, beginning with the evening twilight prayers, according to the prescribed rules, he entered the interior of his palace to dispel the fatigue of the journey. In a pleasant spot within the house—white with plaster, purified by moonbeams, and cooled by the wind—he sat comfortably upon a beautiful, soft bed and fell asleep. His disciples also attended to him by massaging his feet, fanning him, and offering water and betel; then, by his command, they went elsewhere and slept.

Then Mayūrabhaṭṭa, having risen during the *brahmamuhūrta*, meditated upon his chosen deity, prayed to the earth, performed the purification of his body, and put on two clean, washed garments; facing east, with *darbha* grass as a purifier in his hands, having sipped water according to the rules (*svācānta*) and restrained his breath (*prāṇāyāma*), he sat down upon a comfortable seat for the contemplation of the Supreme Self.

Then, as Bāṇabhaṭṭa’s wife—the daughter of Mayūrabhaṭṭa—rose from her husband’s bed and was slowly descending the staircase from the high floor of the palace, she was observed by Mayūrabhaṭṭa. Having seen her, and driven by the impulse of fate, he described her—who possessed such beauty—as if she were another's woman, through eight verses, as follows:

"Who is this young woman who, having finished her meal, goes forth at dawn with disheveled garments and clothes clinging to her limbs with sweat; like a startled deer, she looks about in every direction, filled with apprehension?"
By whom has this lotus-face, with its honey-sweet nectar, been bitten?

By whom has heaven been enjoyed today? Whose left hand is it that, while entwining the mass of hair with its sparse flowers, has struck down the God of Love, who was already slain by the eye of Shiva?
With her upper garment slipped down, her girdle loosened from its fastenings,
and her hair disheveled, she emerged from the bedchamber with a smiling face, holding betel in her left hand; overcome by passion and seeking her lover, she went forth.

Who is this woman with a face like the full moon, fair-complexioned and with eyes like those of a deer; whose gait is like that of a playful lordly elephant in rut or a swan, making the surface of the earth beautiful;
whose mouth is made fragrant and cool by her breath, and who speaks words as soft as nectar?
A man lives as a youth with his own thorn [still within him], he who has such a beloved. //3//
Who is this woman with such beautiful hips, who surpasses even the god of love in her intoxication?
Her curved knitting of the brows rivals the splendor of Indra’s rainbow;
she whose face is like a full moon and a blooming lotus, and whose waist is slender—she is truly beautiful.
The *veṇī* consists of the *indravajrā* and *upendravajrā* meters alternating; the *bhujaṅgaprayāta* consists of the *vibhakti-lalita* meter. //4//
Who is this woman, possessing a face like the shimmering moon through her amorous gestures and expressions,
her body the color of a campaka flower, plump and adorned with ornaments;
and who moves about so boldly and gracefully, like a lioness?
Moreover, she is like a sky-lotus, possessing a face that bestows her own bliss upon those who desire it. //5//
Who is this woman with limbs so exquisitely formed, her eyes tremulous, walking with the grace of a swan;
she whose two hands are smeared with saffron and adorned with golden ornaments, and who makes the anklets ring out as she goes along the path?
Thus she proceeds, her flowers disheveled and her braid trailing as she stumbles.
Holding betel in her left hand, with a smiling face, she entered the secret chamber.
Who is this woman of fresh youth with a moon-like face walking along the lovely path—
her eyes rolling and agitated by sleep, her bimba-fruit lips full,
her hair disheveled, and her body torn by nails and mangled by teeth?
By which Rākṣasa has this Śārdūlavikrīḍita Rati been enjoyed? //7//
Who is this doe, her body firm with the weight of full breasts, marked with turmeric at her waist, wandering alone like one abandoned by her herd,
moving with the languid grace of a rutting lordly elephant? She proceeds with playful ease.
Indeed, upon seeing this form which leads even to the bodiless god [Kāma], even an old man becomes filled with desire. //8//
Then she decorated the interior of the house.

Thereupon, in the body of Mayūrabhaṭṭa—who was an exceedingly learned Vedic scholar and extremely righteous—leprosy suddenly broke out like a drop of ink upon a garment that had been washed clean of all impurity due to a casual sin.
Then, upon his own body...

Beholding this transformation, he quickly descended from his lofty palace, covered himself with a garment, entered the interior of his house, and sat down, reflecting: "Alas! What is this sudden transformation that has occurred in my body?
Surely no sin whatsoever has been committed by me through knowledge or desire since birth."
"I remember.
Let it be for now; rather, I shall reflect upon it further.
Then, having summoned his dear disciple, he said: "Long-lived one, go and [investigate] thoroughly..."
Having reflected, he should come here to the vicinity of our residence; "Whose is this seven-storied mansion, white with plaster and reaching toward the clouds? [he should ask.]

Having said, "So be it," he went there, touched [the ground], and returning, performed a salutation and said, "O Teacher, this is the residence of your son-in-law, Bāṇabhaṭṭa. Upon hearing that, he immediately fell into great distress and thought: "Alas! My daughter was described by me, who am devoid of fortune; this is its fruit. Let it be; from now on, having composed a hymn of praise to the glorious Sun, I shall perform the expiation for his bodily end in order to remove his leprosy."

Having thus resolved, he then said to his dear disciple: "Venerable one, a certain task is being commanded by me; you must perform it entirely within yourself, without hesitation and without deliberation. When he replied, "So be it," he spoke again: "Today is Saturday; I must observe a fast and remain strictly inside."

"Whosoever—whether a royal official or anyone else—comes seeking an audience with me, you must speak to him thus: 'The Guru, exhausted from the journey, ate last night; because his food has not yet been digested, he remains sleeping inside today, afflicted by fever and a headache.

You, along with your circle of disciples, should perform the worship of the deity, the offering of food, the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, and so forth, and then eat at the proper time, as well as your circle of servants."

Food must be caused to be given even to horses, bulls, and the like. At the door of the temple, someone must remain standing firmly so that no one enters within unobserved. Furthermore, none of the disciples shall come into my presence unless summoned by you. You—

Furthermore, you must always remain nearby at a distance that is neither too far nor too near, as is appropriate. Moreover, today you must go to the bank of the Śiprā river, identify a large tree in a secluded spot, and in the evening darkness, fasten a hundredfold rope-sling capable of bearing a heavy load to an upper branch of that tree; many loads of wood must then be brought there. Then, during the latter part of the night, with four disciples on the bed—
"I am asleep as if about to die; I must be carried to that spot.

You too, having taken the materials for the worship of the deity, fresh garments, and fire, must go there. Then, he performed everything exactly as he had been told. Subsequently, when Mayūrabhaṭṭa was brought by them to the bank of the Śiprā during the latter part of the night, he spoke to those disciples: "By you..."

"Having brought the bed, we should go far away and remain there; whoever comes along this path must be turned back. The disciples did exactly as instructed, but they placed the beloved disciple nearby. Having personally performed the purification of the body, bathed, and completed the appropriate rites such as sipping water (ācamana) and breath control (prāṇāyāma), he returned to the foot of a tree, established the sacred fire upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), and adorned it with offerings.
Having cast loads of wood onto the fire and prepared a funeral pyre, he summoned his beloved disciple to his side, covered his own body, and showed it to him, saying:
"Alas! Suddenly a leprosy has appeared on my body; for its removal..."
The glorious Sun is being praised by me;
you should remain not too far away.
"Whatever verse I recite, you must pay close attention and write it down on paper.

Having heard this, he stood nearby together with his disciple. Then Mayūrabhaṭṭa climbed a tree and, standing facing the front of the swing at the break of dawn, composed one verse after another to praise the glorious Sun and cut one rope of the swing after each. The disciple, possessing a retentive memory for a hundred things, took them up immediately and wrote them on paper. In this manner, following the sequence of the rays, the horses, the chariot, the dawn, and the solar orb as previously described, ninety-nine verses were completed.

The cords of the carrying-net were severed by that many [insects], and then, somehow managing to grasp a single cord, he composed the hundredth verse; at that very moment, his body became free of leprosy.

Seeing this, he attained great joy, thinking, "This has been accomplished by the grace of the glorious Sūrya," and began to cut the remaining rope to perform the expiation for the end of his life. Immediately, the Lord Bhāskara, being well-pleased, approached him, took his hand, set him down upon the ground, stroked his body with his own hand, embraced him, and said, "You have become free from sin;
now ask for another boon.
Then he replied, "O Blessed One, this alone is my boon: that you are my inner controller (antaryāmī)."
"It has become manifest. Then the Blessed One said: "With a serene mind, I shall grant this even though it was not requested:

living out the full span of a human life, free from disease, and having enjoyed all worldly pleasures, at the end of the body you shall attain union with me—this applies to whoever [recites] these one hundred verses."
"He shall praise me and be freed from all sins;
by my grace, he will obtain health, excellent poetic talent, intelligence, superior strength, beauty, longevity, knowledge, sovereignty, wealth, and happiness."

Having addressed him in this manner, while he was still looking on, the Blessed One ascended into the sky, trailing a garland of rays. Mayūrabhaṭṭa, thinking, "This is a great favor," performed one hundred and eight prostrations with his limbs touching the ground. Then, at the request of the boon granted by the illustrious Sūrya, he composed a single verse of praise for the fruit [of the ritual]. Then, having performed the morning and midday rites, having worshipped the deity, and having fully honored the consecrated fire—

Having circumambulated [the deity] and prostrated with the eight limbs, and having performed the expiation (*niṣkṛti*) consisting of the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) for the atonement of his bodily end,
he dismissed [the deities]. Surrounded by his disciples and filled with joy, he returned to his own residence, invited the Brahmins, honored them, fed them, and then ate together with his retinue.
And he passed that night with great joy in this very discourse.
Then, with the permission of Mayūrabhaṭṭa—who was delighted by the grace of the illustrious Sūrya—this discourse was brought into the public domain by his disciples. Now...

At an auspicious moment, having dispatched learned men with great respect, King Śrī Harṣa summoned Mayūrabhaṭṭa; and having performed his morning rites, Mayūrabhaṭṭa, accompanied by his disciples, arrived at the royal palace.

The king went out to meet him as far as the palace gate, took him by the hand, and escorted him forward. Leading him into the assembly hall, he seated him upon a most beautiful and lofty throne. Without requiring a formal salutation, the poet offered blessings to the king—who was seated according to protocol—by means of the *Śrīsūryaśataka* alone, to the astonishment of all the members of the assembly.

The two thighs of the king were highly praised by poets and learned men; thereupon, the king, being exceedingly pleased, honored them by bestowing elephants, horses, chariots, villages, dwellings, ornaments, swings, palaces, wealth, and other gifts, and requested that they remain right in his presence.
When [the poet] was granted permission to go home without the customary formal rising in greeting, he departed.
He entered his own residence.

Then, by the king's command, having brought his family from his native land, he settled in the palace granted by the king and, like Bāṇabhaṭṭa, remained there, constantly pleasing King Śrī Harṣa with the fresh lotuses of his own verses. Thus, the *Śrīsūryaśataka* appeared, consisting of one hundred verses plus a single concluding verse of praise for the fruit [of the work]. The meter of these hundred verses is called *sragdharā*. As its definition is stated in the *Vṛttaratnākara*: "That which consists of three *ma*, *ra*, *bha*, *na*, *ya*, and *na* gaṇas, joined with the pauses of the three Munis (7, 5, 7 syllables), is celebrated as *sragdharā*."

In this regard, the distinction should be understood as follows: there is a description of the rays in forty-three verses; then a description of the horse in six verses; then a description of Aruṇa in eleven verses; then a description of the chariot in twelve verses; then a description of the orb in eight verses; then a description of the Blessed Lord in twenty verses; and finally, one verse in praise of the fruit.

The ultimate purport (*paramatātparya*) of all these verses is indeed that which was stated previously—namely, the cessation of what is undesirable and so forth; however, the intermediate purports (*avāntaratātparyāṇi*) will become clear in their respective places. In this regard, the author composes an auspicious invocation (*maṅgala*) consisting of a benediction from the deity Sun, which is characterized by a necessary praise in the form of a reference to the entity known as Indra—who is renowned for being the agent of the destruction of the Daitya Jambha, who was more powerful than the leprosy and obstacles that constitute powerful sins, [all] for the sake of pacifying fear and evil in his own person at the commencement of the work he intends to undertake.

May the two suns, red as if sprinkled by floods of liquid mineral-veins from the slopes of the Eastern Mountain at the same time that the dawn approaches, bring prosperity— those suns which bear the thick vermilion dust arising from the frontal globes of the elephants of the Lord of Jambha.
May the ever-new rays of the Sun shine forth, illuminating the world. //1//
"Jambheti. May the *bhānavīyas*—the rays (*bhānavaḥ*) connected with the sun (*bhānu*)—be for your prosperity (*vibhūtyai*), that is, for your sovereignty (*aiśvaryāya*).

Of what nature are these rays? They are fresh (*abhinavāḥ*), new, arising at the time of dawn (*uṣaḥkāla*). For this very reason, they illuminate (*bhāsayantaḥ*) the world (*bhuvanam*), the earthly realm, by dispelling darkness. For this same reason, they are red (*raktāḥ*, *lohitāḥ*). Here, a threefold poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) is suggested.

Like what? Like one bearing a thick, dense cloud of vermilion powder (*sindūra-reṇu*) that has arisen from the temples (*kumbha*) of the elephant Airāvata—the mount of Indra, the enemy (*arāti*) of the demon Jambha—or like that which arises from the temples of the elephant of the eastern quarter, the enemy of Jambha. Vermilion is applied to the temples of elephants for the sake of beauty.
"What kind?
means that, first, by rising in the eastern direction, they become "watery" (vāruṇa) due to contact with the vermilion situated on Mount Āvarta and the Kumbhasthala mountain.

It was as if sprinkled by the floods—the streams flowing hither and thither due to the connection with waterfalls—of the liquid essence from the rows of minerals such as red chalk (*gaurika*) and realgar (*manaḥśilā*) found on the slopes and edges of the Sunrise Mountain (*udayagiri*). Simultaneously, in such a way that the time was equal to the rays of the sun, it was as if reddened or dyed by the glow—the splendor—of the approaching forest of *kāmalā* flowers;
this is indicated here by the three locations.
In the solar orb, there is a natural vermilion redness;
it is the cause of the night-lotuses' crimson hue, which arises from the flow of mineral streams bearing vermilion dust and the splendor of the lotus groves.

Because it is imagined as a cause, there may be three types of *utprekṣā*—namely, those consisting of a thing (*vastu*), a cause (*hetu*), and a result (*phala*)—according to its definition. Here, the excellence of the poet’s sentiment directed toward the sun is what constitutes the *dhvani* (suggested sense) of the poem; for it is said that "the sentiment (*bhāva*) directed toward gods and so forth is called *rati*," and "the wise declare *dhvani* to be that where the suggested meaning is superior to the expressed. This applies to what follows as well. In the final foot here, there is an alliteration (*anuprāsa*) on the letter *bha*. According to Amara, *bhānu* means both "ray" and "the sun."
The suffix *liṅ* is used in the sense of a benediction (*āśis*) in [the form] "bhūyāsuḥ. //1//
The hollow interior of the lotus-bud hut, for the sake of giving to one bowed down in devotion,
[is filled] with bees dwelling within the hollow of the lotus-bud hut;
[it is] the lotus-bud.

As if desiring to attract the goddess Lakṣmī, they open the lotus groves; may these suns, who are capable of destroying the terror of the world fallen into the darkness of the face of Time, protect you.
May the Lord bring you prosperity; may his hands, with the luster of young sprouts, bring you prosperity in all your actions.
May the rays— the beams— of you, the Sun, who are worthy of praise, likewise bring about your welfare hereafter as well, just as they did before.

Of what nature were they? Those whose luster was like that of *kisalaya*—fresh sprouts—were reddish due to their tenderness because of their recent emergence. It is appropriate that the hands of others who possess auspicious marks are also reddish. [The term] *udghāṭana* means drawing out or pulling.
Even acts such as giving, protecting the frightened, and so forth, are indeed the duties of the hands; this is even a worldly truth.

Who are they? They are those who cause the multitude of lotuses to bloom. Here, a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) is suggested: [the sun] has the desire—the longing—to draw toward itself and seize *lakṣmī*—beauty or prosperity—in order to give it to his own servant who is bowed down by devotion, who is humble with devotion.

For whom [the lotuses] are as if such [as those described]. And this is a *phalotprekṣā* (poetic fancy regarding a result), because there is a conceptualization of the first praised result—the granting of fortune (*lakṣmī*)—following the perception of the blossoming of the lotus grove, which is established by the very nature of the sun’s rays, as being the result itself. The definition has been stated previously. Of what sort [is she]? She is hidden, well-concealed, within the interior—the hollow—of that particular house, namely the hut (*kuṭī*), which is the middle or center of the lotus (*kamalapuṭa*); specifically, within the interior of its inner chamber (*niṣkuha*). Alternatively, [it may mean] she is hidden within the bud (*puṭa*) of the lotus, which is like a golden... [the rest of the sentence is truncated in the source].
Like a hollowed-out casket, like a closed bud— that very lotus-cup which was her hut— within its interior, within its lap,

and even in the center of that interior, she was hidden as if in a bosom; having drawn Lakṣmī out from within by the power of the Lord’s impelling glance, those who delight in being givers of all desired things [bestowed her] upon the supplicant.

The meaning is that they desire to give to the devotee. And since her dwelling is the lotus grove, its blossoming [is required]. It is well known that another man also, having opened [the door] for her who remains hidden within the house, takes hold of her by force and gives her away.

Furthermore, of what nature are they? "Kālākāra" means that whose form (ākāra) or essential nature (svarūpa) is like Kāla—that is, the dark-colored one, or Death (kṛtānta)—because he swallows the world. Of such a darkness, its face (ānana) is the preeminent region; fallen there by fate, whatever fear (sādhvasa) the world possesses, those who are capable (kalpāḥ)—meaning skilled (pravīṇāḥ)—in its destruction (dhvaṃsa), that is, in its annihilation. [Note on grammar: The word "udghāṭanam" is derived from the root *ghaṭ* in the sense of "assembling" (saṃghāte) belonging to the *curādi* class; the form is established with the suffix *uṭ* due to the substitution of *mi* for *tra*. According to Amara, "vali-dvasta-śavaḥ karāḥ. The final result of this analysis is that the verse describes the terrifying power of the Lord's dark form, which, like the face of the all-consuming darkness of cosmic dissolution, strikes terror into the world; yet those who have fallen into that darkness by divine providence are capable of destroying that very fear through their mastery of His nature. For the Kṛtāntas, *has* means "time," and in reality, these are the eons of destruction (*adhvaṃsa-kalpā*).
[Of the Kṛtāntas; of the Kṛtāntas]

This is the reading; however, it is not in verse because it would result in a break in the alliteration (*anuprāsa*). Its meaning is "well-prepared" (*sajjāra*), according to Amara’s lexicon: "The words *kalpa*, *sajja*, and *nirāmaya* [mean 'ready']."
In this case, the absence of limbs and so forth is as previously described. //2//

Falling alike upon the interiors of lotuses and upon the sharp peaks of mountains—[the raindrops]. Upon the interiors of the lotuses... upon the interiors of the lotuses... upon the interiors of the lotuses.

May the rays of the sun protect you— rays that are uniform at the beginning of the day and at the time of its cessation, proceeding without alternation across the courtyard of the mansion of the three worlds,
and bearing intensely the heat born of continuous travel upon the path. //3//
May the rays of the sun— the feet of the radiant one— protect and guard you.
According to Amarasimha, "pāda" refers to a ray and a quarter.

Of what nature were they? They were intensely, utterly hot, bearing—that is, possessing—heat. Here, a poetic fancy (utprekṣā) is suggested: as if produced by the fatigue of the road caused by continuous travel, or the exhaustion from walking through the streets.
And since their activities are of a uniform nature, it is appropriate that they perform the functions of feet.
